card.label: Manchester Baby
card.learning_takeaway: See how cathode-ray-tube storage let an experimental 1948 machine hold and run its own program.
card.card: Manchester's experimental Baby computer tested a way to store data electronically in cathode-ray tubes. Patterns of dots represented binary information, including a program held in memory. Its successful run in 1948 demonstrated a stored-program approach that made changing a task different from rewiring a machine.

evidence.locator: Collection description, CRT memory and first program paragraphs
evidence.note: Checked CRT storage, program-in-memory purpose, and 1948 run; comparison concerns these documented configurations rather than every later version of ENIAC.

evidence.locator: ENIAC being set up; ENIAC tube change
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The museum's stored-program explanation and ENIAC's documented cable-and-switch setup support a historical comparison of how programs were configured.

relations.note: The museum's stored-program explanation and ENIAC's documented cable-and-switch setup support a historical comparison of how programs were configured.

card.label: Complementary distribution
card.learning_takeaway: Recognize nonoverlapping sound environments without assuming this alone proves that the sounds share one phoneme.
card.card: Two sounds have complementary distribution when they occur in nonoverlapping environments. That can help identify allophones, but it is not enough by itself: English /h/ and /ŋ/ also occupy different environments for many speakers. Phonetic similarity and broader patterns help determine whether sounds belong together.

evidence.locator: §4.4, Phones without contrastive distribution; Phonetic similarity
evidence.note: Checked h/ŋ counterexample and need for additional evidence; did not equate complementary distribution automatically with allophony.

evidence.locator: §4.1, The phonological units of spoken language
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source directly contrasts complementary distributions that do and do not justify grouping sounds as allophones of one phoneme.

relations.note: The source directly contrasts complementary distributions that do and do not justify grouping sounds as allophones of one phoneme.

card.label: Grapheme cluster
card.learning_takeaway: Group code points into a best-effort approximation of a user-perceived character for text editing.
card.card: A grapheme cluster groups Unicode code points into an approximation of a user-perceived character. A letter and its combining accents may belong together, letting a cursor move over them as a unit. The default rules are useful but may require tailoring for particular scripts or editing tasks.

evidence.note: Checked approximation, combining-sequence example, and explicit tailoring caveat in UAX 29; not a universal one-cluster/one-glyph equation.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The sources distinguish abstract code points from editing-oriented groups of them; this comparison explains why text length has several legitimate units.

relations.note: The sources distinguish abstract code points from editing-oriented groups of them; this comparison explains why text length has several legitimate units.

card.label: Unicode normalization
card.learning_takeaway: Transform equivalent character sequences into a common binary representation through decomposition, ordering, and optional recomposition.
card.card: Unicode normalization gives equivalent text sequences a common representation. It decomposes characters, orders combining marks, and sometimes recomposes them. The chosen normalization form matters: canonical forms preserve distinctions that compatibility forms may remove, so normalization is more specific than simply making text look alike.

evidence.note: Checked decomposition, ordering, recomposition, and canonical versus compatibility behavior; normalization is not a general visual-similarity matcher.

relations.note: UAX 15 sections 1.1–1.3 explicitly use canonical equivalence to define normalization forms and their transformations.

card.label: Interleaved practice
card.learning_takeaway: Mix different mathematical problem types so learners must select a strategy instead of repeating one blocked routine.
card.card: Interleaved practice mixes different kinds of problems rather than grouping one type into a long block. In the cited mathematics intervention, students had to choose a suitable strategy for each problem. The challenge is partly recognizing which method applies, not simply carrying out a method already signaled by repetition.

evidence.locator: Structured Abstract, Intervention and Control Condition
evidence.note: Checked the mathematics intervention's ordering manipulation and strategy-selection rationale; not claimed effective for every subject or identical to spacing.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Mixing problem types concerns strategy selection, whereas spacing concerns timing of repeated encounters; the sources provide distinct instructional dimensions to compare.

relations.note: Mixing problem types concerns strategy selection, whereas spacing concerns timing of repeated encounters; the sources provide distinct instructional dimensions to compare.

card.label: Atlas linguistique de la France
card.learning_takeaway: See how mapped transcriptions from many places make regional language variation inspectable.
card.card: The Atlas linguistique de la France turned regional speech observations into maps. Around the turn of the twentieth century, fieldwork gathered detailed transcriptions from hundreds of French locations. The atlas shows how systematically placing comparable forms on maps can make geographical variation visible rather than merely listing local words.

evidence.note: Checked survey scale, transcription and mapping; omitted the source's apparent fieldworker-name typo rather than reproducing it.

relations.note: The atlas is a named collection of geographically organized language observations, providing a historical comparison with modern sociolinguistic corpora.

card.label: Betweenness centrality
card.learning_takeaway: Measure how much shortest-path traffic passes through a node or edge rather than simply counting its immediate contacts.
card.card: Betweenness centrality measures a node's or edge's share of shortest paths between other points in a network. When several shortest paths exist, their contribution is divided. This highlights potential intermediary positions that simple neighbor counts miss, while remaining a model of routes rather than a measurement of actual message traffic.

evidence.note: Checked shortest-path splitting and node/edge definitions; hypothetical flow is not claimed to be the route all real information follows.

relations.note: Shortest-path mediation is a specific way to analyze positions in social-network representations, distinct from describing the network or counting direct ties.

card.label: Grace Hopper
card.learning_takeaway: Connect early compiler work and COBOL standardization to efforts to make programming accessible beyond machine instructions.
card.card: Grace Hopper helped develop early compilers and compiler-based languages, then played an important role in defining COBOL. Her career shows a change in programming practice: building tools and shared language specifications that made computers easier to program, rather than treating every task only as machine-level calculation.

evidence.note: Checked early compiler work and the 1959 COBOL role; avoided claiming she alone invented the first compiler or authored SQL.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Hopper's work on easier programming languages and SQL's declarative query design provide distinct examples of tools that let programmers express intent at a higher level.

relations.note: Hopper's work on easier programming languages and SQL's declarative query design provide distinct examples of tools that let programmers express intent at a higher level.

card.label: SQL
card.learning_takeaway: Describe desired query results declaratively while a database planner chooses how to find them.
card.card: SQL lets a program describe the data it wants rather than prescribe every retrieval step. The database's query planner chooses an execution strategy, such as scanning a table or using an index. The same requested result can therefore be produced through different underlying algorithms.

evidence.note: Checked declarative query semantics and planner alternatives; the description is about querying, not every SQL operation or implementation.

relations.note: SQLite's query-planner overview explicitly explains SQL's declarative role and the database engine's choice of retrieval algorithm.

card.label: Covering index
card.learning_takeaway: Include search and output columns in an index so a query need not consult the original table.
card.card: A covering index contains every column a particular query needs, including its output columns. The database can answer that query from the index without looking up matching rows in the original table. Whether an index covers a query therefore depends on that query's requested information.

evidence.note: Checked search-plus-output coverage and eliminated table lookup; an index can cover one query without covering every query.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: This index design changes how a database retrieves selected columns; it is an implementation facet rather than a synonym for the database itself.

relations.note: This index design changes how a database retrieves selected columns; it is an implementation facet rather than a synonym for the database itself.

card.label: Dyad (social group)
card.learning_takeaway: See why a two-person group depends on both members' continued participation and cannot outlast either member's departure.
card.card: A dyad is a two-person social group. Its existence depends directly on both participants: when one leaves, no two-person group remains. This gives the relationship a different structure from a larger group, where some members can continue interacting after another person withdraws.

evidence.note: Checked two-member dependence; not claimed that all social consequences or obligations disappear when a dyad ends.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly contrasts Simmel's two-member and three-member groups by withdrawal and the continuing relationships available.

card.label: Divisional organizational structure
card.learning_takeaway: Place several functions together within product, market, or regional divisions to concentrate accountability locally.
card.card: A divisional structure places several functions together around a product, market, service, or region. Each division can coordinate its own activities and take clearer responsibility for its segment. The tradeoff is that divisions may become isolated, with duplicated systems and weaker coordination across the whole organization.

evidence.note: Checked grouping basis and divisional isolation; did not claim that geographic and product divisions must use identical arrangements.

relations.note: OpenStax explicitly describes divisions as groupings of functional departments and contrasts their local coordination with functional silos.

card.label: Social norms
card.learning_takeaway: Recognize shared expectations for conduct, including unwritten rules learned by observing others and their consequences.
card.card: Social norms are shared expectations about conduct. Some are written and formally enforced, while others are learned through observation and everyday reactions. A person's behavior can follow a norm even without an official watching, because approval, disapproval, and anticipated consequences also help sustain expectations.

evidence.note: Checked formal/informal expectations and social reactions; norms are distinguished from ideals and from a claim that everyone always complies.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The social-reality chapter explicitly defines institutionalization through establishing conventions or norms within society.

relations.note: The social-reality chapter explicitly defines institutionalization through establishing conventions or norms within society.

card.label: Atomic commit
card.learning_takeaway: Make a transaction appear all-or-nothing even though storage writes happen sequentially and can be interrupted.
card.card: Atomic commit makes a transaction's changes appear all-or-nothing, even though storage writes occur one after another. SQLite uses recovery mechanisms to preserve that appearance across crashes or power failures. The guarantee concerns which changes take effect, rather than requiring hardware to write everything simultaneously.

evidence.note: Checked all-or-nothing meaning and sequential hardware writes; crash safety remains subject to the documented storage assumptions.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: SQLite's atomic-commit documentation explains rollback journals as the recovery mechanism used for atomic commit in rollback mode.

relations.note: SQLite's atomic-commit documentation explains rollback journals as the recovery mechanism used for atomic commit in rollback mode.

card.label: Edge embeddedness
card.learning_takeaway: Count the mutual neighbors of a connected pair to describe the social context surrounding their tie.
card.card: Edge embeddedness counts how many common neighbors the two ends of a tie share. Mutual contacts create a social setting around the relationship and may make misconduct more visible. A local bridge has zero embeddedness, connecting people without that immediate shared-neighbor context.

evidence.note: Checked shared-neighbor count and zero case; mutual friends are not claimed to ensure trust or prevent all misconduct.

relations.note: The chapter directly equates zero embeddedness with the local-bridge condition and discusses mutual neighbors' reputational role.

card.label: Password salting
card.learning_takeaway: Add per-password salt before costly hashing to prevent shared passwords from routinely producing identical stored hashes.
card.card: Password salting adds a separate value when a password is hashed for storage. Different salts help prevent equal passwords from routinely producing equal stored hashes. A suitable password-hashing scheme also makes each guess costly; salting and computational expense address different parts of an offline guessing attack.

evidence.note: Checked salt collision minimization, stored salt/hash pair, and cost factor; no claim that salt alone makes weak passwords safe.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: NIST's salted password-hashing process applies cryptographic transformations to password storage rather than encrypting a message for later reading.

relations.note: NIST's salted password-hashing process applies cryptographic transformations to password storage rather than encrypting a message for later reading.

card.label: Insurance deductible
card.learning_takeaway: Require an initial out-of-pocket loss amount before the insurance coverage begins paying.
card.card: An insurance deductible is an amount the policyholder pays before specified coverage starts paying. It leaves some loss with the insured party instead of transferring every cost to the insurer. In the textbook's incentive account, retaining that stake can discourage risk-taking that full coverage might otherwise encourage.

evidence.note: Checked threshold structure and qualified incentive rationale; not advice about an appropriate deductible for any person or policy.

relations.note: The moral-hazard section explicitly identifies deductibles as a cost-sharing method intended to preserve incentives to avoid losses.

card.label: Community-led language reclamation
card.learning_takeaway: Let communities' own language histories and goals guide locally tailored reclamation work rather than assuming one shared language.
card.card: Community-led language reclamation begins with a community's own history and goals. Cenerini's Michif case explains that Métis communities do not all share one language, so a uniform national approach can miss local identities. Learning what people speak and value shapes which reclamation work makes sense there.

evidence.note: Checked the approved local-history/goals condition and multilingual-community qualification; no generic replacement of the baseline revitalization identity.

relations.note: Cenerini's local-history emphasis can guide the purposes of documentation; the link preserves the governance distinction instead of renaming generic revitalization.

card.label: Efficiency wage
card.learning_takeaway: Pay above the reservation wage when the induced effort and reduced turnover can justify the extra wage cost.
card.card: An efficiency wage can exceed the worker's reservation wage because pay changes behavior as well as cost. In the labor-discipline model, a more valuable job encourages effort and makes departure less attractive. A firm weighs the wage bill against the amount of effective work it obtains.

evidence.locator: Section 6.7 Wages, effort, and profits in the labour discipline model, Figure 6.6 and efficiency wages definition; Section 6.4 Employment rents
evidence.note: Checked explicitly as a model, not a universal wage law; distinct from a statutory minimum wage or a claim that raising any wage always pays for itself.

relations.note: The model uses the value at risk from losing a job to connect wages with effort; this applies the employment-rent mechanism to wage setting.

card.label: Common-value auction
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish shared underlying value from bidders' differing information about that value.
card.card: In a common-value auction, the object has the same underlying value to bidders, but they may estimate it differently. A jar of coins is a simple example. Winning can then reveal that one's estimate was unusually optimistic, so the information contained in winning matters for sensible bidding.

evidence.note: Checked shared value versus different estimates and winner information; real auctions can combine common and private components.

relations.note: The Yale lecture introduces the winner's curse through its common-value coin-jar auction and explains conditioning on winning.

card.label: William Labov
card.learning_takeaway: See how occupation, education, and income were used to compare linguistic variant frequencies across social strata.
card.card: William Labov's study of New York speech compared linguistic variation with occupation, education, and income. It also examined differences between casual speech and reading. The case shows how social categories become research variables and why contextual variation must be considered alongside differences between groups.

evidence.note: Checked the three social measures and two contexts; correlations are not described as proof that class causes a pronunciation.

card.label: Multi-column index
card.learning_takeaway: Order index entries by several columns so combined constraints avoid filtering unrelated intermediate matches.
card.card: A multi-column index orders records using several fields together. In SQLite's fruit example, indexing fruit and state lets the database locate California oranges directly instead of first finding all oranges and rejecting other states. Column order determines how that combined ordering can be used.

evidence.note: Checked combined conditions and ordered index columns; no blanket guarantee that any column order accelerates every query.

card.label: Triad (social group)
card.learning_takeaway: See how adding a third member permits coalitions and lets the group persist after one member leaves.
card.card: A triad is a three-person social group. Adding the third member creates possibilities unavailable in a dyad, including two-against-one coalitions and a majority view. If someone withdraws, the remaining pair can still interact, so the group's relationships are not all dependent on one uninterrupted two-person bond.

evidence.note: Checked coalition and withdrawal distinctions; a remaining pair is not inaccurately called a three-person triad.

relations.note: The group-size chapter explicitly contrasts triads with dyads through coalition possibilities and survival of a remaining pair.

card.label: Economics
card.learning_takeaway: Connect choices under scarce resources with the gains and coordination problems of specialization and exchange.
card.card: Economics studies how people and societies make choices when resources are limited. Specialization can increase what people produce, but it also makes them depend on exchange and coordination. Studying those choices includes asking how information, incentives, and institutions affect whether the potential gains are actually realized.
card.original_description: social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services

evidence.note: Checked scarcity and specialization from the introduction and information-related trade obstacles from section 16.1; no claim that monetary value measures every human goal.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The introductory scarcity-and-exchange framework leads to the specific question of how unequal information can obstruct mutually beneficial transactions.

relations.note: The introductory scarcity-and-exchange framework leads to the specific question of how unequal information can obstruct mutually beneficial transactions.

card.label: Rollback journal
card.learning_takeaway: Preserve old database content before overwrite so an uncompleted transaction can be undone.
card.card: A rollback journal saves original database content before a transaction overwrites it. If the transaction must be undone, the saved content can restore the earlier state. This differs from a write-ahead log, which preserves the main database while appending the new changes elsewhere.

evidence.note: Checked old-versus-new content distinction and restoration purpose; not described as a permanent historical audit log.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The saved-original-content mechanism is a concrete way SQLite realizes atomic commit in rollback mode; WAL provides a contrasting mechanism.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The saved-original-content mechanism is a concrete way SQLite realizes atomic commit in rollback mode; WAL provides a contrasting mechanism.

card.label: International Cooperative Alliance
card.learning_takeaway: Explore how an international federation coordinated information, common principles, and trade among otherwise separate cooperatives.
card.card: The International Cooperative Alliance was founded in 1895 to connect cooperatives across countries. Its initial aims included sharing information, defending common principles, and developing international trade. It illustrates how independent member enterprises can coordinate through a federation without becoming a single ordinary business under one owner.

evidence.note: Checked founding aims and cooperative membership; no claim about current membership counts or authority over every cooperative.

card.label: Networked team structure
card.learning_takeaway: Coordinate task-focused teams through flexible relationship networks rather than relying primarily on fixed reporting lines.
card.card: A networked team structure organizes work around flexible connections among task-focused teams. Teams may initially be assigned, then find additional collaborators and resources as the work develops. The distinctive feature is this evolving task arrangement, rather than treating every informal workplace friendship as an organizational design.

evidence.note: Checked the approved task-team distinction from informal organization and the wider organic orientation; no claim that reporting responsibilities vanish.

card.label: Morris worm
card.learning_takeaway: See how self-propagating code disrupted network services without destroying stored files in the 1988 incident.
card.card: The Morris worm spread across the early Internet in 1988 and disrupted computers and services without destroying their files. Its impact illustrates that availability can fail even when stored data remains intact. The incident also prompted organized response efforts, including an early computer emergency response team.

card.label: Fangyan
card.learning_takeaway: Explore how a Han-era collection of regional words preserves evidence used to infer earlier dialect groupings.
card.card: Fangyan is a Han-era collection of regional words associated with the scholar Yang Xiong. By recording different expressions and pronunciations across places, it preserved evidence about linguistic diversity. Later scholars used that material to infer earlier dialect groupings, showing how a vocabulary work can become historical evidence.

evidence.note: Checked regional vocabulary, Yang Xiong attribution, and later scholarly use; no unverified precise date or exhaustive dialect classification is asserted.

card.label: International Phonetic Alphabet
card.learning_takeaway: Use a cross-language sound notation to avoid inconsistencies between ordinary spelling and pronunciation.
card.card: The International Phonetic Alphabet provides a shared notation for speech sounds across languages. It avoids relying on ordinary spelling, where one letter can represent different sounds and one sound can have several spellings. Transcriptions can be broad or include finer detail, depending on the analyst's purpose.

evidence.note: Checked cross-language notation, spelling mismatch and broad/narrow transcription; the alphabet is not an ordinary writing system for one language.

card.label: Delayed judgments of learning
card.learning_takeaway: After a delay, use only a cue to judge future recall so immediate familiarity is less misleading.
card.card: A delayed judgment of learning asks someone to estimate future recall after time away from the material, using a cue without the answer visible. The delay reduces reliance on immediate familiarity. The cited guide treats this as promising for allocating study, while noting limited classroom evidence.

evidence.note: Checked delay, cue-only access, prospective judgment, and low classroom-evidence rating; not equated with an immediate confidence rating or actual test performance.

card.label: Reduplication
card.learning_takeaway: Repeat all or part of a linguistic form to express a grammatical or meaning contrast.
card.card: Reduplication repeats part or all of a linguistic form to express a grammatical or meaning contrast. In Halq'eméylem, one pattern derives meanings such as being disposed to an action. English salad-salad provides a different example: repetition can emphasize a prototypical instance rather than simply pluralizing something.

evidence.note: Checked repeated form, Halq'eméylem disposition example and English prototypicality; meanings of reduplication vary by construction and language.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly lists reduplication among morphological processes beyond affixation and supplies the two contrasting language examples.

card.label: Emergent norm theory
card.learning_takeaway: Explain crowd conduct through locally developing guidelines in unfamiliar situations rather than assuming all crowds act irrationally.
card.card: Emergent norm theory explains crowd behavior through guidelines that participants develop in unfamiliar situations. People bring prior expectations, interact, and may accept new ways of acting as circumstances change. The theory treats crowds as more than irrational masses, while leaving questions about how norms spread and gain acceptance.

evidence.note: Checked explanatory status and the source's unresolved acceptance/spread questions; the theory is not presented as a universally established causal law.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

relations.note: The source explicitly makes changing and newly established norms central to the emergent-norm account of crowds.

card.label: Other-initiated conversational repair
card.learning_takeaway: Signal trouble with another speaker's message so the original speaker can repeat, clarify, or confirm it.
card.card: Other-initiated repair occurs when a listener signals trouble with someone else's message and the original speaker helps resolve it. The response may repeat words, clarify a missing detail, or confirm an interpretation. This creates a brief collaborative detour that repairs understanding before the conversation proceeds.

evidence.locator: Introduction; Materials and Methods, repair-sequence definition
evidence.note: Checked initiator/solution sequence and alternative repair operations; the observed mechanisms are not generalized into claims about every language without qualification.

evidence.locator: Opening; Grounding in Conversation; contribution model
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Repair makes a breakdown explicit, while grounding also includes routine evidence of understanding; the two sources support their connection without making them equivalent.

relations.note: Repair makes a breakdown explicit, while grounding also includes routine evidence of understanding; the two sources support their connection without making them equivalent.

card.label: Structural ambiguity
card.learning_takeaway: Derive different interpretations from alternative phrase attachments while keeping the words unchanged.
card.card: Structural ambiguity occurs when the same words allow different internal groupings. In I saw someone with a telescope, the telescope may be the instrument used for seeing or something the other person possessed. The difference comes from phrase attachment, without requiring a word to acquire another meaning.

evidence.note: Checked both telescope attachments and distinction from lexical ambiguity; no claim that every ambiguous expression has exactly two parses.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The telescope example illustrates why semantic composition depends on how parts are grouped, not only on the meanings of individual words.

relations.note: The telescope example illustrates why semantic composition depends on how parts are grouped, not only on the meanings of individual words.

card.label: Cryptography
card.learning_takeaway: Combine keyed encryption and authentication to protect message confidentiality, integrity, and peer identity.
card.card: Cryptography uses keyed mathematical techniques to protect information and verify messages or participants. Encryption can hide content, while authentication and integrity mechanisms help detect impersonation or alteration. TLS illustrates how several cryptographic tools are combined into a communication protocol rather than relying on secrecy of the design.
card.original_description: Protecting information through mathematical encoding and verification techniques.

evidence.note: Checked TLS security goals and key/design distinction; encryption alone is not claimed to provide every cryptographic property.

evidence.locator: Section I.A, design principle d (open design)

card.label: Sociology
card.learning_takeaway: Connect everyday interactions with patterned relationships and institutions at larger social scales.
card.card: Sociology studies patterns in how people interact, form groups, and organize societies. It connects small encounters with larger institutions and historical conditions. A conflict between work and family responsibilities, for example, can be examined as more than one person's private failure to manage time well.

card.learning_takeaway: Explore why electronic calculation speed coexisted with days of wiring and switch-setting for a new problem.

card.label: Bank of England
card.learning_takeaway: Trace the transition from a privately owned government banker to a nationalized central bank.
card.card: The Bank of England began in 1694 as a privately owned bank helping finance the government. It also accepted public deposits, and much later was nationalized. Its history shows that a public financial role and private ownership can coexist, rather than central banking always beginning with government ownership.

evidence.note: Checked foundation, financing role, deposits and 1946 nationalization; no assertion about current governors, policies or unused legal powers.

relations.note: The Bank's history explicitly connects its government-banking position with competition from the South Sea Company and the 1720 crisis.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:named_subject, risk:qualification_or_assumption, risk:source_asserted_relationship

card.label: Chantale Cenerini
card.learning_takeaway: Learn from her account of documenting community stories while respecting distinct local Michif and Métis language histories.
card.card: Chantale Cenerini describes documenting stories with Michif and Métis communities as work that can preserve language, family histories, and locally valued knowledge. Her account emphasizes learning each community's linguistic history first. A shared national identity does not mean every community uses the same language.

evidence.locator: §9.7, interview on local context and community stories
evidence.note: Checked first-person account and community-specific language histories; no universal claim about every Métis speaker or documentation project's outcome.

relations.note: Cenerini's interview directly describes her story-recording work and its language-documentation and family-legacy purposes.
